Cutaneous manifestations

Why the skin reflects systemic illness and how to describe it

Diagnostic and prognostic role

Skin is immunologically active, vascular and linked to immune, inflammatory, vascular, metabolic, endocrine and neurocutaneous pathways. A lesion may precede familiar systemic symptoms, track activity or organ involvement, and affect pain, itch, appearance, quality of life and self-esteem. Interpret the sign in the clinical context rather than assume it alone establishes a systemic diagnosis.

Layers and lesion depth

Epidermis contains keratinocytes and melanocytes; dermis contains collagen and elastic fibers, hair follicles, vessels and nerves; subcutis is fat. Primary lesions arise on previously normal skin; secondary change follows manipulation or evolution. Loss restricted to epidermis is erosion; loss of epidermis plus dermis is ulcer.

Primary flat, raised, fluid-filled

Macule flat color change <1 cm; patch flat ≥1 cm. Papule raised <1 cm; plaque raised ≥1 cm. Vesicle fluid-filled <1 cm; bulla ≥2 cm in THIS lecture table. Nodule ≥1 cm dome/oval/spherical; tumor ≥2 cm irregular. These thresholds differ from some other dermatology texts and from the user’s pediatric lecture; retain this lecture’s bulla ≥2 cm and tumor ≥2 cm for its own questions.

Secondary morphology

Scale is desquamating stratum corneum; crust dried exudate; lichenification thickened skin with accentuated lines; erosion epidermal surface loss; ulcer extends into dermis. The lecture table labels atrophy a depression with intact skin but inaccurately says “thickening”; interpret atrophy as tissue thinning/loss, and consult original table. Describe site, color and distribution together with type.

Autoimmune diseases

Lupus, dermatomyositis and sclerosis patterns

Cutaneous lupus categories

Lupus erythematosus is autoantibody-associated organ inflammation. LE-specific skin disease divides into acute (ACLE), subacute (SCLE), chronic (CCLE) and can overlap systemic LE; LE-nonspecific non-scarring alopecia and oral ulcers signal activity but occur in other conditions. Lecture estimates 90% with ACLE develop SLE; about 50% SCLE have SLE and 10–15% severe CNS/renal disease; only a few CCLE develop SLE. These are lecture-associated proportions, not diagnostic criteria.

ACLE: malar, generalized and TEN-like

Localized malar butterfly rash: transient non-scarring erythematous plaque across cheeks/nose sparing nasolabial folds, photosensitive, often parallels systemic flare (present at SLE diagnosis in 40–60%). Generalized ACLE: pruritic photodistributed macules/papules, sometimes wider trunk distribution, about 30% SLE in lecture. TEN-like ACLE forms flaccid bullae followed by erosions and widespread peeling. The lecturer first describes dorsal hand involvement at interphalangeal joints yet later notes IP-joint sparing in a photo; rely on the explicit Gottron knuckle contrast when differentiating DM.

SCLE and CCLE

SCLE: erythematous scaly photosensitive plaques, papulosquamous, psoriasiform or annular forms; systemic disease may occur. CCLE: atrophic-centered erythematous facial/scalp plaques, especially discoid LE, with scarring alopecia when scalp follicles are destroyed; photosensitivity and leukopenia association noted. Distinguish non-scarring diffuse alopecia of LE-nonspecific disease.

Dermatomyositis clinical findings

Inflammatory skin disease with or without proximal muscle weakness; 60% concurrent skin/muscle and 30% skin-first in lecture. Pathognomonic Gottron papules are violaceous/erythematous over MCP/IP knuckles; Gottron sign thin violaceous extensor patches on elbows/knees. Heliotrope is edematous violaceous upper eyelid/periorbital patch. V sign chest; shawl upper back; periungual erythema; symmetric lateral hip/thigh holster sign. Facial DM rash may extend into nasolabial folds, unlike malar ACLE. Skin and muscle activity need not parallel. Request CK and EMG when myopathy suspected; EULAR/ACR criteria remain in original appendices. Source labels cutaneous-only “myopathic DM,” an apparent terminology slip; do not equate absence of weakness with proven normal muscle tests.

Scleroderma, morphea and systemic sclerosis

Triad vascular injury, fibrosis and immune dysregulation. Morphea is localized indurated erythematous then depressed/hyperpigmented skin without internal organ involvement; limited 1–2 body parts, linear childhood band (facial en coup de sabre), generalized 2–3 body parts as lecture wording. Systemic sclerosis features puffy fingers progressing to sclerodactyly, Raynaud tricolor episodes and nailfold giant capillaries/microhemorrhages. Limited cutaneous SSc about 66%; diffuse about 33% with proximal/trunk skin and higher lung/kidney/heart/GI risk; overlap syndromes are also listed. Evaluate organ symptoms rather than diagnose systemic disease from hardness alone.

Metabolic syndromes

Visible lipid deposits and cardiovascular risk

Dyslipidemia and xanthomas

Abnormal cholesterol and/or triglycerides increase cardiovascular risk. Tendinous xanthomas reflect lipid-laden dermal cells and are whitish, skin-colored or erythematous nodules on knuckles/tendons. Lecturer cites occurrence in 40–50% of familial hypercholesterolemia. Association is strong but a skin lesion alone does not prove dyslipidemia; order lipid testing and assess family/cardiovascular risk.

Xanthelasma

Smooth yellow thin plaques at medial upper/lower eyelids; common and can occur without lipid disorder. Lecture says about half have underlying dyslipidemia, so request a lipid profile. The Mona Lisa historical discussion contrasts speculative hypercholesterolemia and hypothyroidism interpretations: an illustration of differential diagnosis, not a confirmed medical diagnosis of the painting.

Endocrine disorders

Thyroid, cortisol, adrenal and diabetic clues

Hyperthyroidism versus hypothyroidism

Hyperthyroidism: diffuse hair thinning, warm moist skin, palmar/plantar hyperhidrosis, flushing and pretibial myxedema/thyroid dermopathy (red shin nodules/plaques becoming peau d’orange). Hypothyroidism: xerosis (most common), cold blotchy skin, carotenemia, dry coarse hair/brittle nails, loss of lateral eyebrow third, myxedematous doughy periorbital swelling, macroglossia, thick lips/broad nose. Correlate with thyroid studies; pretibial myxedema is not the same as hypothyroid generalized myxedema.

Cushing syndrome

Chronic glucocorticoid excess can be endogenous (pituitary/adrenal lesion) or drug-induced. Central face/neck/trunk adiposity, moon facies and buffalo hump combine with acne, hair thinning, androgen-dependent hair growth, thin skin, easy bruising, striae and poor wound healing. Systemic hypertension, proximal weakness, mental change and osteoporosis are noted. The lecture repeatedly calls striae white; color alone is not a diagnostic criterion. Investigate glucocorticoid exposure and endocrine cause.

Addison disease

Primary adrenal insufficiency affects glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid secretion. Fatigue, weight loss, myalgia and GI symptoms with bronze hyperpigmentation on sun-exposed face/temples, palmar creases and gums support suspicion. Lecture page 9 also repeats “diffuse hair thinning, warm moist skin and hyperhidrosis” immediately under Addison—apparently carried from hyperthyroidism; the Addison summary table specifically emphasizes pigmentation. Correlate with adrenal testing and clinical severity.

Diabetes: general cutaneous effects

Lecture estimates 30–70% develop a skin problem; xerosis/pruritus and bacterial/fungal infections are common. Acanthosis nigricans with skin tags reflects hyperinsulinemia/insulin resistance in obesity or prediabetes: thick velvety dark plaques on neck/axilla. It does not prove diabetes and has a malignancy differential if abrupt/generalized.

Diabetic dermopathy, necrobiosis and foot

Diabetic dermopathy: common asymptomatic brown atrophic shin macules/patches, often longstanding diabetes (~55% in lecture), marker of microangiopathy; assess retinopathy/nephropathy. The source calls it pathognomonic, but it is best treated as a suggestive clinical clue rather than a stand-alone diagnostic test. Necrobiosis lipoidica: often type 1 DM, annular red-purple sharply bordered leg plaque with atrophic telangiectatic center, possible ulceration and microangiopathy. Foot ulcers at pressure sites result from neuropathy, impaired circulation and poor healing; inspect feet and prevent unnoticed trauma.

Paraneoplastic dermatoses

Timing, distribution and mucosal danger

Malignant acanthosis nigricans

Sudden generalized or rapidly progressive thick hyperpigmented velvety plaques in unusual sites, beyond ordinary neck/axilla folds. Lecture associates most strongly with gastric adenocarcinoma, also hepatocellular, bladder, breast and pancreatic carcinomas; can signal poor prognosis. Assess age, timing and systemic symptoms; ordinary obesity/insulin resistance-associated AN is much more common.

Leser–Trélat sign

Seborrheic keratoses are benign slowly increasing hyperpigmented “stuck-on” plaques on face/back. Abrupt eruption of numerous SKs over weeks/months (Leser–Trélat) prompts malignancy evaluation; lecture mentions GI adenocarcinoma (~30% of associated cancers), breast and lymphoproliferative malignancies and poor prognosis when truly paraneoplastic. Ordinary age-related SKs are common and the sign is not definitive proof of cancer.

Erythroderma / exfoliative dermatitis

Generalized erythematous scaling involving most or all skin. It may follow drug reaction or chronic skin disease (psoriasis most common in added notes, eczema/atopic dermatitis and seborrheic disorders also listed), or an underlying malignancy, especially cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in this lecture. Take medication and prior-dermatosis history, assess extent/systemic illness and investigate cause.

Paraneoplastic pemphigus

Severe potentially fatal autoimmune blistering with painful bullae and erosions of skin and mucous membranes, strongly associated with lymphoproliferative/lymphoreticular malignancy (lecture: 84%; names Hodgkin lymphoma as most common). Promptly evaluate mucosal involvement and underlying malignancy, with specialist care. Contrast simple isolated bullae with painful extensive mucocutaneous disease.

                          ANSWER KEY
  1. B       A macule is a flat, non-palpable lesion smaller
             than 1 cm that results from a change in skin
             color.
  2. C       The malar rash of acute cutaneous lupus
             erythematosus appears over the cheeks and
             nose but characteristically spares the nasolabial
             folds. This helps distinguish it from other facial
             rashes.
  3. B       Gottron’s papules are erythematous or
             violaceous papules found over the knuckles,
             particularly      the     interphalangeal     and
             metacarpophalangeal joints. They are a
             characteristic finding of dermatomyositis.
  4. B       Systemic sclerosis commonly presents with
             Raynaud’s phenomenon, puffy fingers that
             progress to sclerodactyly, and nail-fold capillary
             abnormalities. These findings reflect the
             vascular injury and fibrosis of the disease.
  5. B       Tendinous xanthomas are deposits of
             lipid-laden cells in the skin and tendons and are
             strongly associated with hypercholesterolemia,

Cutaneous manifestations

  • Diagnostic and prognostic role: Skin is immunologically active, vascular and linked to immune, inflammatory, vascular, metabolic, endocrine and neurocutaneous pathways.
  • Layers and lesion depth: Epidermis contains keratinocytes and melanocytes; dermis contains collagen and elastic fibers, hair follicles, vessels and nerves; subcutis is fat.
  • Primary flat, raised, fluid-filled: Macule flat color change <1 cm; patch flat ≥1 cm.
  • Secondary morphology: Scale is desquamating stratum corneum; crust dried exudate; lichenification thickened skin with accentuated lines; erosion epidermal surface loss; ulcer extends into dermis.

Autoimmune diseases

  • Cutaneous lupus categories: Lupus erythematosus is autoantibody-associated organ inflammation.
  • ACLE: malar, generalized and TEN-like: Localized malar butterfly rash: transient non-scarring erythematous plaque across cheeks/nose sparing nasolabial folds, photosensitive, often parallels systemic flare (present at SLE diagnosis in 40–60%).
  • SCLE and CCLE: SCLE: erythematous scaly photosensitive plaques, papulosquamous, psoriasiform or annular forms; systemic disease may occur.
  • Dermatomyositis clinical findings: Inflammatory skin disease with or without proximal muscle weakness; 60% concurrent skin/muscle and 30% skin-first in lecture.
  • Scleroderma, morphea and systemic sclerosis: Triad vascular injury, fibrosis and immune dysregulation.

Metabolic syndromes

  • Dyslipidemia and xanthomas: Abnormal cholesterol and/or triglycerides increase cardiovascular risk.
  • Xanthelasma: Smooth yellow thin plaques at medial upper/lower eyelids; common and can occur without lipid disorder.

Endocrine disorders

  • Hyperthyroidism versus hypothyroidism: Hyperthyroidism: diffuse hair thinning, warm moist skin, palmar/plantar hyperhidrosis, flushing and pretibial myxedema/thyroid dermopathy (red shin nodules/plaques becoming peau d’orange).
  • Cushing syndrome: Chronic glucocorticoid excess can be endogenous (pituitary/adrenal lesion) or drug-induced.
  • Addison disease: Primary adrenal insufficiency affects glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid secretion.
  • Diabetes: general cutaneous effects: Lecture estimates 30–70% develop a skin problem; xerosis/pruritus and bacterial/fungal infections are common.
  • Diabetic dermopathy, necrobiosis and foot: Diabetic dermopathy: common asymptomatic brown atrophic shin macules/patches, often longstanding diabetes (~55% in lecture), marker of microangiopathy; assess retinopathy/nephropathy.

Paraneoplastic dermatoses

  • Malignant acanthosis nigricans: Sudden generalized or rapidly progressive thick hyperpigmented velvety plaques in unusual sites, beyond ordinary neck/axilla folds.
  • Leser–Trélat sign: Seborrheic keratoses are benign slowly increasing hyperpigmented “stuck-on” plaques on face/back.
  • Erythroderma / exfoliative dermatitis: Generalized erythematous scaling involving most or all skin.
  • Paraneoplastic pemphigus: Severe potentially fatal autoimmune blistering with painful bullae and erosions of skin and mucous membranes, strongly associated with lymphoproliferative/lymphoreticular malignancy (lecture: 84%; names Hodgkin lymphoma as most common).
